title: Medical and sales representatives
author: Editorial Desk
summary: An often overlooked white-collar workforce with a BMS federation.
body:
The **Bharatiya Medical & Sales Representatives' Mahasangh** is one of the 38 federations listed on the website of Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh (BMS). It represents people who work as medical representatives and sales promotion staff, mainly in pharmaceutical and consumer goods companies. They are a white-collar workforce that is easy to overlook. They carry a bag, not a spanner, and they are rarely pictured in a labour demonstration. Yet they are workers in the full sense: they depend on a salary, they work to targets set by others, and they can lose their jobs in a merger. This post explains the law that has applied to them, how it changed in November 2025, the issues they raise, and why fair practice in their line of work is a public concern as well as a labour one.

## A special law, now replaced

For nearly fifty years the main statute was the **Sales Promotion Employees (Conditions of Service) Act, 1976**. Courts have held in many cases that medical representatives are not workmen under that definition, because their work is specialised sales promotion and not manual, skilled, technical or clerical labour in the sense of the old law, and the Delhi High Court has restated this view. The 1976 Act therefore extended to them the benefits of several labour laws. According to a summary of the Act, these included the Industrial Disputes Act, the Minimum Wages Act, the Payment of Gratuity Act, the Payment of Bonus Act and the Maternity Benefit Act, together with earned leave, medical leave and a written appointment letter. It first applied to the pharmaceutical industry and was extended in 2011 to ten more industries.

The position changed with the labour codes that came into effect on 21 November 2025. According to a labour-law summary, the 1976 Act was repealed and its subject is now dealt with in the **Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020**, which treats sales promotion employees as workers and preserves leave entitlements such as earned leave at one day for every eleven days of duty. The same employees are also treated as workers under the Industrial Relations Code, which gives them a clearer path to raise a dispute. The Code on Wages applies to their minimum wages, timely payment and bonus, and the Code on Social Security covers provident fund, employees' state insurance, gratuity and maternity benefit. Under that Code, permanent staff are entitled to gratuity after five years and fixed-term staff on a pro-rata basis after one year. The coverage is no longer limited to listed industries: it extends to sales promotion employees in any establishment within the scope of the codes, and managers and supervisors earning above a stated wage ceiling are excluded.

This was not a neutral change for the federation. In January 2019, when the Government amended the rules under the 1976 Act, the Mahasangh protested at Jantar Mantar and met the Union Labour Minister. Its memorandum asked, among other things, that any work involving sales or business promotion fall under the Act, that managerial and supervisory staff earning up to Rs 25,000 a month be included, that new categories of fixed-term, temporary, apprentice and trainee employment not be introduced, and that employers should not impose one-sided contracts. The debate over coverage, wage ceilings and fixed-term employment continues under the new codes, and the federation's concerns are worth following as the rules are implemented.

## Issues

The employees' concerns arise from the nature of the job.

- **Targets and incentives.** Pay often has a large variable component tied to sales targets, which may be raised from year to year. A medical representative whose territory changes or whose product loses market share can see income fall sharply.
- **Termination and retrenchment during mergers.** When pharmaceutical companies merge or restructure, overlapping field forces are reduced. Without the protection of industrial dispute law, the worker has had little recourse except the contract.
- **Working hours.** Field work does not end at a fixed hour, since reports, calls and travel extend the day. Some States have acted: a Tamil Nadu order reported in November 2019 set working hours for medical and sales representatives from nine to five with a lunch break, capped weekly hours at 54 including overtime, and provided overtime at double the normal wage.
- **Digital detailing and technology.** Video calls, e-detailing and data dashboards change how representatives meet doctors. These tools may reduce travel, but they can also increase monitoring and be used to justify fewer jobs.
- **Social security for contract staff.** Employees engaged through third-party agencies may find that their provident fund, insurance and gratuity are not paid or recorded, because the principal employer and the agency each point to the other.

## Why the sector matters beyond its own workers

Medical representatives link doctors with products. They are an important channel through which information on medicines reaches prescribers, and the pressure on them to produce sales can create pressure on ethical practice. Fair and ethical conduct in that link matters to patients as well. In March 2024 the Government notified the **Uniform Code for Pharmaceutical Marketing Practices, 2024**, which bars pharmaceutical companies and their agents from giving healthcare professionals or their relatives personal gifts or any financial or in-kind benefit, from paying for their travel to conferences, and from providing hospitality such as lodging or fine dining, with an exception for those who take part as speakers in recognised medical education programmes. The Department of Pharmaceuticals has also asked industry associations to set up ethics committees and complaint portals. A code of this kind affects the representative directly. A worker who is told to meet impossible targets and also told not to use inducements is in a difficult position unless the company's own targets are realistic. That is why the working conditions of representatives and the ethics of marketing are connected, and why a strong workers' voice helps ethical practice, not hinders it.

## What the federation asks

Taking together the federation's stated positions and the issues above, its demands can be summarised as follows: that the protection once given by the 1976 Act should not be diluted by the new codes; that all employees engaged in sales promotion be covered, including those on lower-paid managerial and supervisory grades; that employment on fixed terms or through third parties should not become a way of avoiding responsibility; that there be effective grievance machinery, including in small establishments; and that working hours, targets and incentives be reasonable and transparent.

## What remains to be done

The first task is clarity: the rules under the new codes should be read closely, and workers and employers should be told plainly what has changed, so that nobody loses a right through misunderstanding. The second is enforcement, since a right to raise a dispute is of use only if the worker knows where to go. The third is dialogue between companies, industry associations and unions on targets, working hours and the use of technology, with the ethics code as a common reference.

## The lesson

White-collar workers also need unions. In the age of targets and dashboards, stress is a safety issue. A worker who is measured every day against numbers that he or she cannot control suffers a real harm, even if no machine is involved, and the law of working conditions is slowly learning to recognise it.
